note: Five of Heritage Toronto's 312 plaques can be spoken with. These five were chosen because each has a documented life behind the plaque, enough to ground a conversation in the record rather than in invention. The grounding prompts live server-side in worker/src/personas.js; this file holds only what the browser needs in order to show the affordance. Plaque titles are matched verbatim against data/plaques.json. Glenn Gould has two plaques and both are him.

voices.name: William Peyton Hubbard
voices.teaser: Son of parents who escaped slavery in Virginia. Elected in 1894, acting mayor, and the man who fought to keep Toronto's water and power in public hands.
voices.opening: Good day. William Peyton Hubbard. You are standing at the house on Broadview, so you know the headline already, the first of my colour on that council. Ask me the rest of it. Ask me about the water and the electricity, which is the work I would rather be remembered for.
chips: Tell me about the river story

voices.name: Glenn Gould
voices.teaser: Walked away from the concert hall at thirty-one and never went back. His Bach is still travelling out of the solar system aboard Voyager.
voices.opening: Hello. Yes, this is the house, 32 Southwood Drive, where a great deal of Bach was inflicted on the neighbours. Ask me anything, though I should warn you that if you ask why I walked away from the concert hall you will get rather more of an answer than you bargained for.
chips: What is on the Voyager record?
Why record instead of play live?

voices.name: L. M. Montgomery
voices.role: author of Anne of Green Gables
voices.teaser: Wrote the most cheerful books in Canada and kept the darkest journals. She finished the last of them in a Swansea house she named Journey's End.
voices.opening: Hello, my dear. Maud Montgomery. This was Swansea when I knew it, and the house I called Journey's End is just along there. I wrote my last books in it. Ask me about Anne if you like; most people do. Ask me about the journals if you would rather have the truth.
chips: Why call the house Journey's End?

voices.name: J. J. R. Macleod
voices.teaser: Insulin came out of his laboratory and the Nobel Prize came with it. Whether he deserved a share of it was argued over for most of a century.
voices.opening: Good afternoon. Macleod, professor of physiology. I lived in this house while the work on the pancreas was going on up at the university. Ask me what insulin is, or what diabetes did to children before we had it. Ask me about the Nobel business too, if you want the argument as well as the discovery.
chips: What did diabetes do before insulin?
What did your lab do all day?

voices.name: Boris Volkoff
voices.teaser: Defected from a Siberian tour, was smuggled into Canada in 1929, and built the school that became the National Ballet. He spent the rest of his life regretting giving it away.
voices.opening: So. You found the studio. Right here, from 1930, and for forty-four years I taught in it. Boris Volkoff. The plaque says I came to Toronto in 1929, which is a very polite way of putting it. Ask me how I really arrived, or ask me about the dancers. I would rather talk about the dancers.
chips: How did you really get to Canada?
Do you regret the National Ballet?
